title: SpecPrefetch: Parameter-Efficient Expert Prefetching for Sparse MoE Foundation Models

images.desc:
1 Introduction


Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) and vision language models (VLMs) has been driven by scaling model capacity, training data, and computation. However, dense scaling increasingly strains inference cost, memory capacity, and serving throughput. Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures provide an attractive alternative by expanding total parameter capacity while activating only a small subset of experts for each token. Modern MoE models organize expert computation through pure routed expert pools or shared plus routed expert designs (Qwen Team, 2025; Jiang et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2024). Despite architectural differences, both designs expose the same deployment bottleneck. Sparse activation reduces per token computation, but the full expert pool must still be stored or made accessible during inference. As foundation models move from cloud datacenters to commodity GPUs and edge platforms, this storage-computation gap becomes a critical bottleneck under limited memory, and local compute.


Expert offloading provides a natural response to the dense expert footprint of MoE models under memory constrained deployment. Instead of keeping the entire expert pool resident on the accelerator, offloading places inactive experts in CPU memory or host-side storage and transfers selected experts to the active device on demand. However, expert demand is not known statically. In each MoE layer, the top-kk experts are determined only after the preceding hidden states are computed and evaluated by the router. As a result, expert transfer cannot be issued until the routing decision becomes available, which serializes hidden state computation, routing, host-to-device transfer, and expert execution along the inference critical path. Thus, the central challenge is not only reducing transfer cost, but also revealing expert demand early enough to overlap transfer with ongoing computation.


Figure 1: 
Comparison of expert-transfer strategies in offloaded MoE inference.



As shown in Figure 1, existing approaches mitigate exposed expert-transfer latency from three perspectives, but their design choices introduce different limitations. Transfer-cost reduction methods, such as quantization and compression, reduce the communication volume of expert movement (Yan et al., 2025). However, they do not alter the timing at which expert demand becomes available: required experts are still identified only after native top-KK routing, so expert transfer remains serialized after routing and can still lie on the critical path before expert execution. Training-free prefetching methods, represented by FATE, exploit cross-layer routing regularity to anticipate expert demand without parameter updates (Fang et al., 2025b). While lightweight and portable, their prediction accuracy depends on stable routing correlations, which may not consistently hold across model architectures, tasks, and modalities. Training-based prediction methods estimate expert activations using auxiliary predictors, parameter-efficient tuning, draft modules, or pre-gating mechanisms (Hwang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Leviathan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024). Although these methods can improve expert recall, coupling prediction with routing or execution may perturb the original expert activation pattern and potentially affect model behavior. Therefore, an effective prefetching solution should predict next-layer expert demand early for transfer scheduling, remain parameter-efficient, and preserve native routing for final expert selection.


To address these limitations, we propose SpecPrefetch, a parameter-efficient prefetching framework for offloaded MoE inference. SpecPrefetch formulates prefetching as next-layer expert prediction: given the representation at layer ll, a shared lightweight adapter predicts a compact candidate set for layer l+1l+1. The candidates are used only for asynchronous host-to-device transfer, while the native router at layer l+1l+1 still selects the final top-KK experts for execution. By decoupling transfer prediction from execution routing, SpecPrefetch improves expert availability without altering pretrained routing semantics. At runtime, a window-aware scheduler turns predicted candidates into feasible transfer decisions by considering prediction confidence, cache residency, and transfer completion time. We validate SpecPrefetch through both offline expert prediction experiments and real-device mobile evaluation. Across Qwen- and DeepSeek-style MoE architectures, SpecPrefetch improves next-layer expert coverage with low trainable overhead; on a mobile device, it further translates prediction gains into practical latency reduction under storage-constrained offloaded inference.


To summarize, we make the following contributions:


• 

We identify learned transfer-only prefetching as a distinct design point for offloaded MoE inference.



• 

We develop SpecPrefetch, a lightweight adapter-based framework that predicts next-layer experts and schedules feasible asynchronous transfers under runtime constraints.



• 

We validate SpecPrefetch through offline prediction experiments and real-device mobile evaluation, showing higher expert coverage, low trainable overhead, and practical latency reduction.

3 Method


SpecPrefetch is a parameter-efficient prefetching framework for offloaded MoE inference that anticipates the expert demand of layer l+1l+1 from the router input available at layer ll. As illustrated in Figure 2, the predicted candidates are used only for asynchronous transfer preparation, while the native router still selects the final top-KK experts during execution, so SpecPrefetch hides exposed transfer latency without changing the routing semantics of the pretrained MoE model. Following this design, Section 3.1 first formulates router-preserving next-layer expert prefetching as a transfer-only prediction problem; Section 3.2 then introduces a lightweight next-layer gate calibration module to estimate expert priorities of layer l+1l+1 from the representation available at layer ll; and Section 3.3 finally describes a window-aware runtime scheduler that converts predicted priorities into feasible asynchronous transfers under cache, queue, and bandwidth constraints.


Figure 2: 
Overview of native MoE execution and SpecPrefetch.
(a) Native MoE routing selects experts only during execution.
(b) SpecPrefetch predicts next-layer candidates for asynchronous transfer, while the native router determines the final executed experts.




3.1 Router Preserving Expert Prefetching


Consider an MoE model with LL MoE layers and EE routed experts per layer. Let 𝐗b,sj∈ℝD\mathbf{X}^{j}_{b,s}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote the router input of token (b,s)(b,s) at layer jj. The native router RjR^{j} selects the token-level top-KK expert set




𝒯b,sj=TopK​(Rj​(𝐗b,sj)),\mathcal{T}^{j}_{b,s}=\mathrm{Top}_{K}\left(R^{j}\left(\mathbf{X}^{j}_{b,s}\right)\right),



and the batch-level expert demand is




𝒯j=⋃b,s𝒯b,sj,\mathcal{T}^{j}=\bigcup_{b,s}\mathcal{T}^{j}_{b,s},



where 𝒯j\mathcal{T}^{j} denotes the batch-level native expert demand at layer jj.


Given an anchor layer ll, SpecPrefetch predicts a candidate expert set for the next MoE layer:




𝒞l+1=Pl​(𝐗l),|𝒞l+1|≤M,\mathcal{C}^{l+1}=P^{l}\left(\mathbf{X}^{l}\right),\quad\left|\mathcal{C}^{l+1}\right|\leq M,



where PlP^{l} is the next-layer expert predictor and MM is the prefetch budget. The candidate set 𝒞l+1\mathcal{C}^{l+1} is used only for early expert transfer. The executed experts are still determined by the native router at layer l+1l+1, which produces the actual demand 𝒯l+1\mathcal{T}^{l+1} from 𝐗l+1\mathbf{X}^{l+1}.


Let tlpredt_{l}^{\mathrm{pred}} denote the time when prediction is issued at layer ll, and let tl+1exect_{l+1}^{\mathrm{exec}} denote the time when layer l+1l+1 begins routed expert computation. The available prefetch window is




Wl=tl+1exec−tlpred.W_{l}=t_{l+1}^{\mathrm{exec}}-t_{l}^{\mathrm{pred}}.



A prediction is useful only when a required expert e∈𝒯l+1e\in\mathcal{T}^{l+1} is resident in accelerator memory before tl+1exect_{l+1}^{\mathrm{exec}}. Since 𝒞l+1\mathcal{C}^{l+1} controls only expert placement, false positives may waste transfer or cache capacity, and false negatives may require on-demand loading. Neither case changes 𝒯l+1\mathcal{T}^{l+1}. Therefore, SpecPrefetch preserves native routing computation while changing only expert transfer timing.




3.2 Adapter-Based Expert Prediction


We implement the predictor PlP^{l} with a single lightweight external adapter shared by the prediction branch. The pretrained MoE forward path is kept frozen, including all native routers and routed experts. Given the router input at layer ll, the adapter estimates the expert priorities of layer l+1l+1 only for prefetch ranking. It does not calibrate, replace, or participate in the native router during execution.


Let 𝐗b,sl∈ℝD\mathbf{X}^{l}_{b,s}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote the router input of token (b,s)(b,s) at layer ll. The shared adapter predicts next-layer expert logits through a low-rank mapping:




𝐳^b,sl+1=𝐁𝐀𝐗b,sl,\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{l+1}_{b,s}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}^{l}_{b,s},



where 𝐀∈ℝr×D\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times D} and 𝐁∈ℝE×r\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times r} are shared across all anchor layers. This introduces r​(D+E)r(D+E) trainable parameters in total. The predicted next-layer expert probability is then computed as




𝐏^b,sl+1=softmax​(𝐳^b,sl+1).\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{l+1}_{b,s}=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{l+1}_{b,s}\right).





During training, the original MoE model follows its native forward path. The frozen router at layer l+1l+1 provides the detached teacher distribution




𝐏Tl+1=softmax​(𝐗l+1​𝐖gl+1⊤),\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{T}}^{l+1}=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\mathbf{X}^{l+1}\mathbf{W}_{g}^{l+1\top}\right),



where 𝐖gl+1∈ℝE×D\mathbf{W}_{g}^{l+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times D} is the native gate weight of layer l+1l+1. The shared adapter is trained to approximate this next-layer routing distribution using only the representation available at layer ll:




ℒNLP=∑l∑b,smb,s​KL​(𝐏T,b,sl+1∥𝐏^b,sl+1)∑b,smb,s.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NLP}}=\sum_{l}\frac{\sum_{b,s}m_{b,s}\,\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{T},b,s}^{l+1}\|\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{b,s}^{l+1}\right)}{\sum_{b,s}m_{b,s}}.





At runtime, token-level probabilities are aggregated into batch-level expert priorities:




sel+1=∑b,smb,s​P^b,s,el+1.s_{e}^{l+1}=\sum_{b,s}m_{b,s}\hat{P}_{b,s,e}^{l+1}.



The candidate expert set used for prefetching is selected by




𝒞l+1=TopM​({sel+1}e=1E).\mathcal{C}^{l+1}=\mathrm{Top}_{M}\left(\{s_{e}^{l+1}\}_{e=1}^{E}\right).



Thus, a shared adapter predicts next-layer expert candidates for prefetching, while frozen native routers determine the executed experts.




3.3 Window-Aware Runtime Scheduling


Finally, the window-aware scheduler turns predicted next-layer expert priorities into asynchronous host-to-device transfers. For each anchor layer ll, it receives the priority scores {sel+1}e=1E\{s_{e}^{l+1}\}_{e=1}^{E} and candidate set 𝒞l+1\mathcal{C}^{l+1}. The scheduler maintains the resident expert set 𝒢​(t)\mathcal{G}(t), the pending transfer set 𝒰​(t)\mathcal{U}(t), and the transfer queue 𝒬​(t)\mathcal{Q}(t), with each expert indexed by the layer-expert pair (l+1,e)(l+1,e).


At scheduling time tt, the scheduler estimates whether each candidate can arrive before the target layer begins routed expert computation. Let t^l+1exec\hat{t}_{l+1}^{\mathrm{exec}} denote the estimated execution time of layer l+1l+1, and let c^el+1​(t)\hat{c}_{e}^{l+1}(t) denote the estimated completion time for transferring expert ee. The feasibility indicator is




ϕel+1​(t)=𝕀​[c^el+1​(t)≤t^l+1exec].\phi_{e}^{l+1}(t)=\mathbb{I}\left[\hat{c}_{e}^{l+1}(t)\leq\hat{t}_{l+1}^{\mathrm{exec}}\right].



The runtime priority combines prediction confidence, cache status, pending-transfer status, and transfer feasibility:




qel+1​(t)\displaystyle q_{e}^{l+1}(t)
=sel+1⋅𝕀​[(l+1,e)∉𝒢​(t)]\displaystyle=s_{e}^{l+1}\cdot\mathbb{I}\!\left[(l+1,e)\notin\mathcal{G}(t)\right]





⋅𝕀​[(l+1,e)∉𝒰​(t)]⋅ϕel+1​(t).\displaystyle\quad\cdot\mathbb{I}\!\left[(l+1,e)\notin\mathcal{U}(t)\right]\cdot\phi_{e}^{l+1}(t).



The scheduler submits candidates with nonzero priority in descending qel+1​(t)q_{e}^{l+1}(t) order until the transfer queue is full. Submitted experts enter 𝒰​(t)\mathcal{U}(t) and are moved to 𝒢​(t)\mathcal{G}(t) after transfer completion.


When execution reaches layer l+1l+1, experts already in 𝒢​(t)\mathcal{G}(t) are executed immediately; otherwise, they are loaded on demand. We measure prefetch effectiveness by ready recall:




ReadyRecalll+1=|ℛl+1||𝒯l+1|,ℛl+1={e∈𝒯l+1:(l+1,e)∈𝒢​(tl+1exec)}.\begin{gathered}\mathrm{ReadyRecall}^{l+1}=\frac{\left|\mathcal{R}^{l+1}\right|}{\left|\mathcal{T}^{l+1}\right|},\\
\mathcal{R}^{l+1}=\left\{e\in\mathcal{T}^{l+1}:(l+1,e)\in\mathcal{G}\!\left(t_{l+1}^{\mathrm{exec}}\right)\right\}.\end{gathered}



Ready recall measures the fraction of native-router-selected experts that are resident before routed expert computation begins. Since the scheduler only controls expert placement, unused prefetches or on-demand loads affect efficiency but not the pretrained MoE output.

Parameter overhead comparison.


To examine whether the recall gains come from larger predictors, Table 4 compares the trainable parameter overhead of different predictor designs. On DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny, SpecPrefetch uses 1.63M trainable parameters, which is only 0.07M more than Single MLP, but far smaller than Draft Model and ProMoE with 26.40M and 32.69M parameters. This corresponds to only 6.2% and 5.0% of their trainable parameter counts, respectively.


The advantage is more evident on Qwen3-VL-MoE-30B. SpecPrefetch uses 12.95M trainable parameters, compared with 24.38M for Single MLP, 19.19M for Draft Model, and 414.45M for ProMoE. In particular, SpecPrefetch requires only 3.1% of the trainable parameters of ProMoE. These results indicate that SpecPrefetch improves next-layer expert prediction through parameter efficient adapter based calibration rather than predictor scaling, which is essential for prefetching because predictor overhead should not offset the latency saved by asynchronous transfer.
